GALEN, ON THE POWER OF PURGATIVE DRUGS. It seems that the most ancient of the physicians left pernicious opinions unrefuted for the same reason that the most ancient of the lawgivers also left the greatest offences unpunished. For since vice was more moderate in that time, and people neither undertook to commit the greatest wrongs nor brought themselves to the most flagrant shamelessness, how could anyone either have prescribed a punishment for things that had never happened at all, or have brought a refutation against things that no one had said at all?

But since, as vice grew over time, nothing was any longer either undared or unsaid among men, the lawgivers devise many new kinds of punishment for wrongdoers, and those who honour truth devise many-sided forms of refutation against the sophists. This is what we too, it seems, would now do, refuting those who abolish the attractive faculty of purgative drugs for the humours that they evacuate, and who claim instead that these drugs have a certain transformative faculty over everything that comes near them, all alike. Nothing was said by Hippocrates against such an opinion. For in his time there was not yet either Asclepiades, who openly behaved shamelessly and stripped, as if for some prize, to contend against the truth, or Erasistratus, who acted with a certain modesty but overturned the whole main point itself, which manifestly holds concerning purgative drugs. For Erasistratus nowhere in his own writings recognises the attractive faculty, the most active and most proper faculty of nature, but rather uses in its place the following toward what is being emptied.

The power in purgative drugs is a part of the power that attracts what is proper to each thing, just as is also the power by which bile is separated off, and urine, and many other things that are brought about by nature both in the health of animals and in the cures of diseases and in the diseases themselves, by physicians and, not least, by nature itself. Since, then, Hippocrates said nothing against those who abolish attraction from among the things that exist, because the doctrine had not yet found a champion as reckless as many of those after them turned out to be, it would be just for us to contend for the truth in place of Hippocrates: first to recall what sort of thing these men say, and then next to show that they do not speak correctly. Their argument, then, is as follows. The purgative drug alters whatever humour it touches into its own particular form. One produces yellow bile, which they call cholagogue; another, likewise, produces phlegm, which they call phlegmagogue; another renders a certain watery nature, which they call hydragogue; and another makes black bile out of whatever humour it touches.

Unit K11.326 (K. XI 326). ENGLISH:
To put it briefly, what is called purgation is, according to their argument, a change and alteration of all the humours in the veins, not an evacuation of one of them. But if this is what you would have, let us now say to them that, whether someone takes a drug that draws bile, or phlegm, or black [bile], or serous fluid, all the humours are evacuated from the veins. And indeed, then, purging someone with such a drug differs from evacuating the blood by cutting a vein only in this respect: in phlebotomies it is excreted just as it was present beforehand, whereas in purgations it has been changed not only in colour but also in consistency. For the drug that draws watery [humours] makes everything in the veins fluid and thin, even if it happened previously to be very thick; that which draws black [bile], conversely, makes everything thick and stagnant, even if it was before very fluid. And accordingly our choice between phlebotomizing and purging will be made according to certain other aims, but it will not be made according to the very kind of the things evacuated. What, then, are the other aims?

Many are readier for venesection than others are, some for purgation, just as others, again, would sooner suffer anything whatever than be venesected. Some would rather submit to having some part of the body cut off than swallow a drug. And indeed some have their stomach upset by purgative drugs, while others take them without distress. Thus you have not only conceded attraction, but have also, far worse than you ought, declared it to be not only of what is proper but simply of all things. Whatever is naturally disposed to purge black bile evacuates black bile straightaway from the beginning. This very thing holds also for those that purge out phlegm and yellow bile. For each of them attracts its proper humour from the beginning, but thicker in the course of time; it is not the case, as you suppose, that a person first filled a whole basin with serous residue, then next another with yellow bile, and then another with phlegm, and that only then is the black evacuated. From which it is clear that what is proper is attracted by the drug, while the watery matter floating on the surface follows along with it.
